2I OurBigBook.com
Starting with x0​=x>0, the continued-fraction algorithm sets
an​=⌊xn​⌋,xn+1​=xn​−an​1​
(12)
unless xn​ is already an integer. This gives
x=[a0​;a1​,a2​,…].
(13)
Every finite continued fraction is rational, since it is built from integers by finitely many additions and reciprocals. Conversely, if x=p/q is rational in lowest terms, then
qp​=a0​+qr​,0≤r<q.
(14)
When r=0, the next complete quotient is q/r. Thus each step is an application of the Euclidean algorithm and replaces the denominator by a smaller nonnegative remainder. The process must terminate. This proves the termination criterion for a simple continued fraction.
For x=3​,
a0​=1,x1​=3​−11​=23​+1​,a1​=1,
(15)
and
x2​=x1​−11​=3​+1,a2​=2.
(16)
Finally,
x3​=x2​−21​=3​−11​=x1​,
(17)
so the complete quotients repeat. Hence the continued fraction of the square root of three is
3​=[1;1,2​]​.
(18)

3K (Coding & Cryptography)

Words: 181 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 181
3K OurBigBook.com
A binary linear-feedback shift register of degree d has a state
(sn​,…,sn+d−1​)∈F2d​ and recurrence
sn+d​=ad−1​sn+d−1​+⋯+a0​sn​.
(19)
Its feedback polynomial is
f(X)=Xd+ad−1​Xd−1+⋯+a0​.
(20)
There are 2d states, and the zero state is fixed. A nonzero periodic orbit therefore visits at most the other 2d−1 states, proving the period bound for a linear-feedback shift register.
For a maximal orbit with d>1, the all-one state cannot itself be fixed. From that state the incoming bit is a0​+⋯+ad−1​ in F2​. If an odd number of the ai​ were one, the incoming bit would be one and the all-one state would be fixed. Hence an even number of the ai​ are one; including the leading coefficient, the feedback polynomial has an odd number of nonzero coefficients. This is the feedback-polynomial parity condition for maximal period.
The given prefix has seven consecutive zeros followed by a one. Any register of degree at most seven would therefore enter the all-zero state before producing the final one, which is impossible. Degree eight is attained by
sn+8​=sn​,
(21)
with initial state 10000000. It produces the next bit 1 and has feedback polynomial
f(X)=X8+1​.
(22)
Thus this is the minimal linear-feedback shift register for the prefix 100000001.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

For the regular concatenation grammar, let
P1​={α→β∈P:β∈/Σ∗}∪{α→wS′:(α→w)∈P, w∈Σ∗}.
(25)
Then define
Hreg=(Σ,V∪V′,P1​∪P′,S).
(26)
If G and G′ are regular, every nonterminal rule retained from P is right-linear, and each replaced terminal rule is also right-linear. A regular derivation in G uses exactly one terminal rule, at its final step; the replacement transfers control to S′, after which a word of L(G′) is generated. Hence
L(Hreg)=L(G)L(G′).

5K (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 145 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 145
5K OurBigBook.com
For a model with k fitted parameters, the Akaike information criterion is
AIC=−2ℓ(θ)+2k,
(36)
where ℓ is the log-likelihood evaluated at the maximum-likelihood estimate.
In the normal linear model with known σ2,
−2ℓ(β)=nlog(2πσ2)+σ21​∥Y−Xβ∥2.
(37)
The maximum-likelihood estimator is the ordinary least-squares estimator, with fitted mean μ​=HY, where
H=X(XTX)−1XT.
(38)
Since only the p components of β are fitted,
AIC=nlog(2πσ2)+σ21​∥Y−μ​∥2+2p.
(39)
After multiplying by σ2 and discarding the model-independent constant, this is exactly Mallows Cp:
Cp​=∥Y−μ​∥2+2pσ2​.
(40)
To compare it with prediction error, write Y=μ+ε and Y∗=μ+ε∗, where μ=Xβ, the two errors are independent, and both have covariance σ2I. Since Hμ=μ, H is an orthogonal projection of rank p, and
Y∗−μ​=ε∗−Hε.
(41)
The cross term has zero expectation, so
MSPE=E∥ε∗∥2+E∥Hε∥2=nσ2+pσ2.
(42)
On the other hand,
E∥Y−μ​∥2=E∥(I−H)ε∥2=σ2tr(I−H)=(n−p)σ2.
(43)
Therefore the unbiased prediction-error identity for ordinary least squares gives
E(Cp​)=(n−p)σ2+2pσ2=(n+p)σ2=MSPE​.
(44)

g′(x)=r+ke−λx(1−λx).

The Laplace integral method for a differential equation seeks
y(z)=∫C​eztf(t)dt.
(53)
Differentiating under the integral and substituting into
zy′′+y′−zy=0
(54)
gives
∫C​ezt[z(t2−1)f(t)+tf(t)]dt=0.
(55)
Since zezt=∂t​ezt, integration by parts yields
[ezt(t2−1)f(t)]∂C​−∫C​ezt[(t2−1)f′(t)+tf(t)]dt=0.
(56)
It is therefore enough to choose f and C so that
(t2−1)f′(t)+tf(t)=0
(57)
and the boundary term vanishes. Solving the first-order equation on −1<t<1 gives
f(t)=1−t2​K​.
(58)
Take C to be the interval [−1,1]. Although f has integrable endpoint singularities,
(t2−1)f(t)=−K1−t2​
(59)
vanishes at both endpoints, so the boundary term is zero. Thus
y(z)=K∫−11​1−t2​ezt​dt.
(60)
At z=0, substituting t=sinθ gives
∫−11​1−t2​dt​=π.
(61)
The normalization y(0)=1 therefore sets K=1/π. By the defining regularity and normalization of the modified Bessel function, this proves the real integral representation of the modified Bessel function I0:
I0​(z)=π1​∫−11​1−s2​ezs​ds​.
(62)

a OurBigBook.com
The Jacobi identity for the Poisson bracket is
{F,{G,H}}+{G,{H,F}}+{H,{F,G}}=0​.
(63)
For quantities with no explicit time dependence,
F˙={F,H},G˙={G,H}.
(64)
If F and G are conserved, the first two terms of the Jacobi identity vanish. Hence
{H,{F,G}}=0,
(65)
or, by antisymmetry,
{{F,G},H}=0​.
(66)
Thus the poisson bracket of conserved quantities is itself conserved.

A subset A of a metric space X is a nowhere dense set when
intA=∅.

The Baire category theorem says that if X is a complete metric space and G1​,G2​,… are open dense subsets of X, then ⋂n≥1​Gn​ is dense in X. Equivalently, no nonempty open subset of X is a countable union of nowhere-dense sets.
To prove it, take a nonempty open set V. Since G1​ is open and dense, there is a closed ball
B(x1​,r1​)⊂V∩G1​

32A OurBigBook.com
A map is Devaney chaos when:
  • every pair of nonempty open sets eventually overlap under an iterate, which is topological transitivity;
  • it has dense periodic points; and
  • nearby initial conditions can eventually separate by a fixed amount, which is sensitive dependence on initial conditions.
Write a point as a binary expansion
x=0.b1​b2​b3​…2​.
(421)
Apart from the harmless choice of expansion at dyadic rationals, the binary shift representation of the doubling map is
F(x)=0.b2​b3​b4​…2​.
(422)
Every open interval contains a binary cylinder specified by a finite initial word. Given cylinders U and V, choose a binary sequence beginning with the word for U and place the word for V after it. A suitable iterate shifts the second word to the front, proving topological transitivity.
Given any cylinder, repeat its defining word forever. The resulting point is periodic and lies in that cylinder, so periodic points are dense.
Finally, given x and any neighbourhood, choose N so large that changing only digits after the first N stays inside that neighbourhood. Choose the later tail so that after N shifts it is either 0 or 3/4, whichever is farther from FN(x). The separation is at least 3/8, so any smaller fixed constant, for example δ=1/4, proves sensitivity. Hence the doubling map is chaotic in Devaney's sense.

n⋅(D+​−D−​)=0​,n⋅(B+​−B−​)=0​,
(512)
and
n×(E+​−E−​)=0​,n×(H+​−H−​)=0​.
(513)
Thus tangential E and H are continuous, as are normal D and B.
Because D=ϵE, the normal electric field generally jumps according to
ϵ+​E+,n​=ϵ−​E−,n​.
(514)
The tangential displacement field generally jumps because ϵ+​=ϵ−​. Since the permeability is common, continuity of tangential H is continuity of tangential B; together with normal-B continuity, every component of B is continuous. The same common μ also makes the normal component of H continuous.

Choose the interface as x=0 and write the incident, reflected, and transmitted fields as plane waves with wavevectors kI​,kR​,kT​. The boundary conditions must hold for every tangential coordinate and every time. The phase matching at a planar wave interface therefore requires
ωI​=ωR​=ωT​
(515)
and equality of tangential wavevectors:
(kI​)∥​=(kR​)∥​=(kT​)∥​.
(516)
The incident and reflected waves are in the same medium, so
∣kI​∣=∣kR​∣. Equality of their tangential components gives
∣kI​∣sinθI​=∣kR​∣sinθR​,
(517)
hence
θR​=θI​​.
(518)
At fixed frequency, ∣k±​∣=ω/v±​ is proportional to the refractive index n±​. Tangential phase matching between incident and transmitted waves gives the Snell law for electromagnetic waves:
∣k−​∣sinθI​=∣k+​∣sinθT​,
(519)
or
n−​sinθI​=n+​sinθT​​.
(520)
Here n±​=c/v±​=cϵ±​μ​ if the vacuum speed c is used to normalize the index.

Take the plane of incidence to be the xy-plane, so all three electric polarizations point along z. Write their signed scalar amplitudes as EI​,ER​,ET​. Tangential-E continuity gives
EI​+ER​=ET​.
(521)
For each plane wave,
H=μω1​k×E.
(522)
Continuity of its tangential component gives
n−​cosθI​(EI​−ER​)=n+​cosθT​ET​,
(523)
where the common proportionality between ∣k∣ and n cancels. Solving the two equations gives the transverse-electric Fresnel reflection coefficient
EI​ER​​=n−​cosθI​+n+​cosθT​n−​cosθI​−n+​cosθT​​.

Using Snell's law to eliminate θT​,
n+​cosθT​=n+2​−n−2​sin2θI​​.

Since ϵ+​>ϵ−​ and μ is common, n+​>n−​. Therefore
(n+​cosθT​)2−(n−​cosθI​)2=n+2​−n−2​>0.
(526)
The numerator is consequently strictly negative throughout
0≤θI​≤π/2, and
∣EI​∣∣ER​∣​=n+2​−n−2​sin2θI​​+n−​cosθI​n+2​−n−2​sin2θI​​−n−​cosθI​​>0​.
(527)
Thus transverse-electric polarization has no Brewster angle in this setting.

The linearized Ricci tensor and scalar obey

The momentum equation is
ρ(∂t​u+(u⋅∇)u)=f+∇⋅σ,∇⋅u=0.
(542)
Taking its scalar product with u gives
∂t​(21​ρ∣u∣2)+∇⋅(21​ρ∣u∣2u)=u⋅f+∇⋅(u⋅σ)−σ:∇u.
(543)
For the Newtonian fluid stress tensor σ=−pI+2μe, its contraction with the velocity gradient is
σ:∇u=2μe:e,
(544)
because incompressibility removes the pressure term and the symmetric rate-of-strain tensor is orthogonal to the antisymmetric part of ∇u. Integration over D and the divergence theorem therefore give the kinetic-energy balance for an incompressible Newtonian fluid:
dtd​∫D​21​ρ∣u∣2dV+∫∂D​21​ρ∣u∣2u⋅ndS=∫D​u⋅fdV+∫∂D​u⋅σ⋅ndS−2μ∫D​e:edV.
(545)
The terms are respectively the rate of change of kinetic energy, outward advective flux of kinetic energy, power supplied by the body force, power supplied by surface traction, and irreversible viscous dissipation. Since f=−∇ψ, the body-force power may also be written −∇⋅(ψu) and interpreted as exchange with potential energy.

a OurBigBook.com
The Householder-John theorem states the following. Let
A=M−N
(562)
be a splitting in which A is Hermitian positive definite. If
B=M∗+N
(563)
is also Hermitian positive definite, then M is nonsingular and every eigenvalue of H=M−1N has modulus less than one. Hence the associated stationary iteration converges.
First, M must be nonsingular. If Mx=0 for some nonzero x, then Nx=−Ax, and therefore
x∗Bx=x∗(M∗+N)x=−x∗Ax<0,
(564)
contradicting the positive definiteness of B.
Now let Hx=λx with x=0. Then Nx=λMx, so
Ax=(1−λ)Mx.
(565)
Put a=x∗Ax>0 and m=x∗Mx. Since λ=1,
m=1−λa​.
(566)
Consequently,
0<x∗Bx=m+λm=a(1−λ1​+1−λλ​)=a∣1−λ∣21−∣λ∣2​.
(567)
It follows that ∣λ∣<1. Thus ρ(H)<1, proving the theorem.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

Solution

Words: 99
b OurBigBook.com
Write
A=D+L+U,
(568)
where D=diag(a1​,…,an​) and L,U are the strict lower and upper triangular parts. The Jacobi method is
x(k+1)=D−1(b−(L+U)x(k)),
(569)
with iteration matrix
H=−D−1(L+U).
(570)
Here A is symmetric, so U=LT. Regard the iteration as the splitting
A=M−N,M=D,N=−(L+LT).
(571)
Let
S=diag(1,−1,1,−1,…).
(572)
Because A is tridiagonal, changing alternating signs reverses the sign of every off-diagonal entry while preserving every diagonal entry. Therefore
MT+N=D−L−LT=SAS.
(573)
Since ST=S=S−1 and A is positive definite, SAS is positive definite. The Householder-John theorem now gives
ρ(H)<1.
(574)
The Jacobi iterates therefore converge to the unique solution A−1b for every starting vector, which is the jacobi convergence for a symmetric positive-definite tridiagonal matrix.
